title: The Three-Lifetime Wrong
author: Zhanran

inline.s: Answer: Because one practices in this life, one enjoys blessed rewards in the next, and then, relying on that fortune, commits evil — leading to a fall in the life after that

. Even if one’s hell-karma is exhausted, one is then reborn among hungry ghosts and animals, and to regain a human body is harder than hard! Therefore the World-Honored One, holding up earth in his hand, asked Ānanda: “Is there more earth in my hand, or more in the great earth?” Ānanda replied: “The great earth holds more.” The Buddha said: “Those who attain a human body are like the earth in my hand; those who lose a human body are like the earth of the great ground.” Hence “through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand births, there is no one to rely upon”! Therefore, if a practitioner does not end birth and death in this very life, then after three lifetimes the suffering and evil retribution are endless — and so it is called the “three-lifetime wrong.”
Master Yinguang, in his Dharma Words from the Shanghai Assembly for Protecting the Nation and Dispelling Calamity, related a real example of the three-lifetime wrong:

“During the Qianlong and Jiaqing reigns of the Qing dynasty, there were three monks who practiced the Chan school, fellow cultivators and companions in the Way. After the three died, one was reborn in Jiangsu and was named Peng Yunzhang; one was reborn in Yunnan and was named He Guiqing; one was reborn in Shaanxi and was named Zhang Fei. Among these three, only Peng Yunzhang could still remember the events of his former life. Later, when he went to the capital to sit the examinations, he met the other two and spoke of how the three of them had been monks in a former life. Although the other two could not remember it, they too felt at first sight as though they were old friends, and so they became inseparable companions. In the palace examination (the highest examination of the civil service, held in the great hall of the palace and presided over by the emperor himself, in which the first place is the zhuàngyuán, followed in order by the bǎngyǎn, tànhuā, and chuánlú), Peng Yunzhang placed first as zhuàngyuán, He Guiqing placed as bǎngyǎn, and Zhang Fei placed as chuánlú. Peng Yunzhang once left the capital to serve as a chief examiner in the provinces, but he was quite given to lust and later died at home. He Guiqing became governor-general (zhìtái, an alternate title for viceroy) at Nanjing; when the Taiping rebellion broke out and Nanjing fell, he was condemned to death by the Qing emperor. Zhang Fei even served as tutor to the Xianfeng emperor; when the Muslim population rose in revolt, they lured him out and killed him. These three men were hardly ordinary monks, yet it is a pity that they did not know to seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land. Although they attained some worldly fortune, two of them did not meet a good end, and Peng actually gave himself to lust — in the lives to come, he may well fare worse than he did in this one!”

“Mr. Wu Yinzhi of Suzhou, a tànhuā of the Qing dynasty, was excellent in learning, virtue, and bearing. In the tenth year of the Republic, he came to pay homage at Mount Putuo and saw me. He himself said that in a former life he had been a monk in Yunnan. As he was only a passing pilgrim offering incense, we could not talk at length, and I did not ask him in detail about the matter. In the eleventh year of the Republic, I went to Yangzhou to carve printing blocks for sutras, and stayed at the home of a disciple in Suzhou; I took the opportunity to seek him out, thinking that his memory of past causes was not yet lost. Who would have thought that when we met and spoke of the matter, he had already completely forgotten it, and from then on there was no further contact. In the nineteenth year of the Republic, I closed myself in retreat at Bao Guo Monastery in Suzhou. In the eleventh month of that year, Mr. Wu came to Bao Guo Monastery together with Li Yinquan and Li Xiehe (Liejun). I asked: ‘How do you know that in a former life you were a monk in Yunnan?’ He said: ‘When I was twenty-six, I had a dream in which I arrived at a monastery, and knew that it was a certain monastery in a certain county of Yunnan. The halls, rooms, trees, and their shapes that I saw all seemed familiar, and I felt myself to be a monk of that monastery. When I woke I still remembered it clearly, and wrote it down item by item. Later a friend of mine went there to take up an official post (Mr. Zhang Zhongren still knew this man’s name), and took my record to compare with the place point by point — not the slightest difference.’ I said: ‘Sir, you are already eighty years old this year; your remaining days are few. You should resume the practice of your former life as a monk — single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the West, so as not to let go to waste the hard work of your former-life cultivation.’ He said: ‘What is so special about reciting the Buddha’s name?’ I said: ‘Reciting the Buddha’s name may not be special, but in this world not many people can do it. The most unspecial thing of all is eating, yet in the whole world there is not one person who does not eat. Why do you still do this most unspecial thing?’ He could not answer, but still he did not agree. He then turned to the two Mr. Lis who had come with him and asked: ‘Do you two gentlemen also recite the Buddha’s name?’ They answered: ‘We do.’ Still he had no further word, and to the end he would not recite the Buddha’s name. On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, just as the lamps were about to be lit, he passed away — having just turned eighty. This gentleman, too, must have had considerable cultivation in his former life, which is why he received great fame and long life in this one. But in this life he merely fulfilled the ordinary moral duties, and no longer even believed in the Buddhadharma — truly lamentable!”
The Elder Master Xuyun, in his Autobiographical Chronology of Master Xuyun, also related an instance he encountered personally:

“Prefect Chen Lanqing, whose ancestral home was Shaoxing in Zhejiang, grew up in Kunming. He took refuge with Monk Yanqi of the West Mountain in Kunming, devoted his mind to reciting the Buddha’s name, and constantly upheld the Diamond Sutra. He was skilled at painting orchids and crabs, and people competed to treasure his works. In his early years, when he returned to his native place to sit the examinations, he felt on first arriving in Hangzhou as though he were in his old home; suddenly he recalled that in a former life he had been a monk of Manao (Agate) Monastery by West Lake. He once described to friends in advance the conditions of the monastery, the furnishings of the old dormitory room where he had lived, and even the flowers and trees in the courtyard, all in vivid detail. The group suspected him of speaking falsely (dàn, to deceive), and badgered (

, to pester) him to go to the monastery — and indeed it was exactly as he had said. He also said that his wife, in a former life, had been the shopkeeper’s wife of a wooden-fish shop beside Manao Monastery, and had once offered a kāṣāya robe, which formed the bond of their present marriage; when people heard this they believed and marveled all the more. His blessed rewards in this life were very ample, and he had several dozen descendants; though he believed in the Buddha and recited the Buddha’s name, he had no intention of donning the black robe (

, the monk’s robe) again. In the thirtieth year of the Guangxu reign, I (Xuyun) was staying at Fuxing Monastery in Kunming; we often came and went together, and though I admonished him many times he would not awaken. A sutra says: ‘For the rich and honored it is hard to study the Way.’ What a pity!”
